title: Philippines adopts national AI governance framework and creates AI council
excerpt: An executive order signed on 12 November 2026 sets six principles for AI, including safety and accountability, and creates a National AI Council. It adds no new penalties.

sources.title: Office of the President of the Philippines: Executive Order No. 131, Adopting the Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework and Creating the National Artificial Intelligence Council (PDF, via Newsbytes.PH)
GizGuide: Executive Order No. 131 on the AI Governance Framework and National AI Council (16 November 2026)

body_html:
The Philippines has adopted a national framework for governing artificial intelligence and set up a council to coordinate it. Executive Order No. 131, signed by the President on 12 November 2026, puts the framework into effect across government. An executive order is a directive from the President to government agencies. It is not a law passed by Congress.

What the order does

The order has two main parts.

  • A governance framework. It lists six principles for AI: transparency and explainability, security and safety, accountability and integrity, human centricity, fairness and equity, and sustainable development.
  • A National Artificial Intelligence Council. The council is chaired by the Executive Secretary, the head of the President's office. Its vice-chair is the Secretary of the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development, which also runs the council's secretariat. Members include the secretaries for information and communications technology, science and technology, trade, finance, education, labour and budget, the heads of the higher education and technical skills agencies, and one private-sector representative.

The council will align government AI programmes with the framework, issue implementation guidelines, set up working groups and recommend measures to the President. These include protections for workers and learners affected by changes that AI brings to jobs. According to GizGuide's summary, the council will report on progress every quarter and the framework will be reviewed at least every two years.

A risk-based toolkit, not new rules

The order includes what it calls a risk-based policy toolkit. Measures must be in proportion to the risk, and they may include guidelines, AI impact assessments, regulatory sandboxes (supervised spaces to test new products), legal reviews and complaint and grievance mechanisms.

It does not create risk categories, licensing or penalties. It says: "Existing sector regulators shall continue to exercise their respective mandates under applicable laws." In practice, bodies such as the National Privacy Commission keep enforcing the Data Privacy Act of 2012 as before.

What is not in it

The order has no specific provisions on human oversight of AI systems, on reporting AI incidents, or on high-risk uses such as AI in hiring, credit or physical robots. "Human centricity" is named as a principle but not defined further. Privacy is not one of the six principles, though the order says AI systems must be consistent with data privacy laws. The order takes effect once published in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation.

Why it matters for staying in charge

Many countries are starting with coordination and principles before passing binding AI laws. The Philippine order follows that path. Its value will depend on what the council's guidelines say, and whether impact assessments and complaint routes become real tools that people can use.

The principles touch several Humasure Directives. Accountability matches D9 Accountable: someone answers for what an AI system does. Security and safety match D3 Physical safety and D6 Secure and supported. Fairness and equity match D8 Fair treatment. A complaint and grievance mechanism, if built, would give people a way to raise problems, which is part of staying in charge.
